title: Pauri 36, meaning: the realm of effort
hookLine: knowledge blazes; then comes the realm of effort, where beauty shapes mind and understanding (Japji 36)

cards: Watch someone learn the violin. The first month is painful for everyone in the house: squeaks, scratches, a bow that won't sit straight. But something is happening that you can't hear yet.
The fingertips are hardening. The ear is learning to catch a note that's slightly off. Six months in, the student hears music differently, not just plays it differently.
Anyone who has trained for anything, a sport, a language, a craft, knows this. You work on the thing, and the thing works on you. Pauri 36 calls the next realm a workshop where exactly that happens.

teach.h: SARAM KHAND — THE LANGUAGE IS BEAUTY.
teach.b: After knowledge blazes, the stanza turns: saram khandd kee baanee roop. The language of Saram Khand is beauty, is form.
Then: tithai ghaarrat gharreeai bahut anoop. There, shaping is done, beyond compare. Gharreeai is what a potter or a smith does, forming something by hand.
And what gets shaped? Tithai gharreeai surat mat man budh.
There, awareness, intellect, mind and understanding are shaped. Not clay. You.

In the realm of knowledge, you saw how big creation is. Here, the seeing gets worked into who you are. In the middle comes a small, honest admission: taa keeaa galaa katheeaa naa jaahi, je ko kahai pichhai pachhutaae.
Its matters can't be told; whoever tries will be sorry afterward. Even Nanak refuses to over-describe it. So what does saram mean?
Here, teachers honestly differ. Many translators read it as effort or striving, from an old word for labor; that's today's title.
Others hear modesty or humility, the same word you met in Pauri 28, where modesty was the yogi's begging bowl. Some read it as spiritual joy.
Sikh teachers often hold these together: the humble, beautiful work of being reshaped.
Either way, the picture is a workshop, where patient, humble effort lets knowledge reshape the mind.

how: Many Sikhs recite Japji Sahib each morning; Pauri 36 describes Saram Khand, the third of the five realms, which Sikh teachers variously explain as the realm of effort, of humility, or of spiritual joy, where the mind itself is reshaped.

o: the realm where effort reshapes the mind
the realm where the hardest workers rest
a realm of riches kept for the wealthy

games.q: what's inside Pauri 36 — tap the pairs.
p: whoever tries to tell it regrets it

s: many read effort; others hear modesty or humility, or spiritual joy.
in Saram Khand, the mind itself is what gets shaped
tithai gharreeai surat mat man budh.
Pauri 36 says whoever tries to describe this realm will regret it
je ko kahai pichhai pachhutaae: words fall short here, and the stanza says so.

games.q: you've entered the workshop of Saram Khand. what is being shaped there?
o: nothing: it's a place of rest.
games.why: tithai gharreeai surat mat man budh: the one being shaped is you.

practice: Picture one small thing you usually rush, washing a pan, writing a message, tying your shoes, listening to someone, and see yourself doing it slowly and well, the way a craftsperson would.
Then give the same care to your breath: in fully, out completely, each breath well made.

wordCard.voice: Saram Khand. The realm of effort, a workshop where beauty is the language and awareness, mind and understanding are shaped. The third of Japji's five realms.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: the realm of saram, read as effort, humility or spiritual joy; the third of Japji's five realms.

carryVoice: Your line: effort shapes the mind. In this workshop, the one being shaped is you. That's day two hundred twenty-five.
